enrichment.short_title: Insurance jurisdiction, lis pendens and anti-suit injunction in cargo claim
key_facts: Evialis SA, a French company and assignee of Ametra, claimed an indemnity under a marine cargo insurance policy against four Italian insurers after cotton pellets were damaged in transit.
Parallel proceedings were brought in Italy by the insurers seeking non-liability declarations and in England by Evialis for indemnity, jurisdiction declarations and an anti-suit injunction.
The parties disputed whether an English jurisdiction clause in the insurance certificate was effective under the Brussels Regulation insurance rules and Italian law.
Andrew Smith J held Evialis had a good arguable case that the English court had jurisdiction, but ordered a stay under Article 27 because the Italian court was first seised.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Applications in concurrent English and Italian proceedings concerning jurisdiction, a stay under Article 27 of the Brussels Regulation, and an anti-suit injunction.
enrichment.outcome: English proceedings stayed; Evialis's application for an anti-suit injunction dismissed.
enrichment.ratio: Where insurance proceedings involving the same cause of action are pending in Italy first, the English court must stay its proceedings under Article 27 of the Brussels Regulation even if there is a good arguable case for English jurisdiction; an anti-suit injunction should not be granted to restrain the Italian proceedings.
legal_issues: Whether the insurance contract contained an effective English jurisdiction agreement under Articles 13 and 14 of the Brussels Regulation
Whether Article 27 required a stay because Italy was the court first seised
Whether an anti-suit injunction restraining Italian proceedings was available or compatible with European law
Construction of the open cover and certificate under English and Italian law

enrichment.short_title: Whether converted flats at Ealing are a house in multiple occupation
key_facts: Mr Stanley converted 5 Mount Avenue, Ealing into eleven self-contained flats and Ealing Borough Council served notices under sections 352 and 372 of the Housing Act 1985.
The owner argued the building was no longer a house but eleven separate houses, so Part XI HMO controls did not apply.
The county court judge held the premises were a house in multiple occupation.
The owner said HMO status would reduce the freehold value by about £500,000 and raised Article 1 Protocol 1.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal from Brentford County Court on a preliminary point whether the premises were an HMO.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed with costs; permission to appeal refused.
enrichment.ratio: A building originally constructed or adapted for occupation by a single household that is now divided into self-contained flats can still be a house for section 345(1) of the Housing Act 1985; the 1989 addition of section 345(2) did not overturn Okereke v Brent on that point.
legal_issues: Whether a converted block of self-contained flats is a house in multiple occupation under section 345
Effect of section 345(2) added by the Local Government Act 1989
Whether Okereke v Brent London Borough Council remained binding authority
Whether Part XI controls breached Article 1 Protocol 1

enrichment.short_title: Sovereign loan negative pledge and pari passu injunction refused
key_facts: Kensington International, assignee of unpaid syndicated loan debt owed by the Republic of the Congo since 1984, obtained summary judgment for about $56.9 million from Cresswell J.
The claimant sought injunctions enforcing negative pledge and pari passu clauses to restrain Congo from granting preferential security over oil revenues, especially via SNPC.
Congo did not appear; the Attorney General appointed an amicus and the court examined State Immunity Act constraints on injunctive relief.
Tomlinson J refused injunctive and declaratory relief, holding enforcement would require coercing third parties and was disproportionate.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Trial of remaining issues after summary judgment on the debt claim, with amicus curiae appointed by the Attorney General.
enrichment.outcome: Injunctive and declaratory relief refused; money judgment already obtained remained.
enrichment.ratio: Even where a sovereign borrower's negative pledge clause is clear and breached, the court may refuse injunctive relief where compliance could realistically be achieved only by coercing third parties, the claimant withholds material information about its acquisition of the debt, and damages or ordinary execution are the appropriate remedies.
legal_issues: Meaning and enforceability of negative pledge and pari passu clauses in sovereign loan agreements
Whether section 13 of the State Immunity Act barred injunctive relief despite clause 19.3 consent
Whether Congo had validly been served and whether assignments were effective
Discretionary grounds for refusing novel injunctive relief against a foreign state

enrichment.short_title: Release date after licence recall and time unlawfully at large
key_facts: Prisoner S was automatically released on licence, then detained in hospital under section 3 of the Mental Health Act 1983 before his licence was revoked under section 39(2) of the Criminal Justice Act 1991.
He absconded from hospital briefly and the Prison Service extended his licence expiry date under section 49(2) of the Prison Act 1952.
Maurice Kay J quashed the recall for failure to consult hospital doctors, but gave guidance on calculating the revised release date.

The Court of Appeal held a recalled licensee can be unlawfully at large without knowing of revocation and that hospital detention under section 3 does not count as lawful custody for section 49 purposes.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal on moot release-date issues after judicial review quashed the licence revocation; Home Secretary did not pursue appeal against quashing.
enrichment.outcome: Court ruled on all three release-date issues in favour of the Secretary of State, but no substantive order made because the recall remained quashed.
enrichment.ratio: A prisoner whose licence is revoked is deemed unlawfully at large under section 39(6) of the 1991 Act even if unaware of revocation; detention in hospital under section 3 of the 1983 Act does not count as lawful custody for section 49(2) of the 1952 Act; absence is computed in whole days.
legal_issues: Whether a patient detained under section 3 of the Mental Health Act 1983 is at large after licence revocation
Whether ignorance of licence revocation prevents time counting as unlawfully at large
How partial days of absence should be calculated under section 49(2)

enrichment.short_title: Equal sharing in short childless working marriage ancillary relief
key_facts: Mr and Mrs Foster, both aged 33, had a short childless marriage during which they built a property portfolio worth about £395,000 net.
The wife earned substantially more than the husband but both worked throughout the marriage.
The district judge returned pre-marital contributions and divided profits equally; the circuit judge increased the wife's share to 70%.
The husband appealed, arguing the district judge's equal-profit approach was correct.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Second appeal to the Court of Appeal with permission on whether financial contributions in a short childless marriage should be weighed unequally.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; district judge's order restored and wife ordered to pay husband's costs from 4 May 2002.
enrichment.ratio: In a short childless marriage where both spouses worked and pooled efforts in a joint property enterprise, White v White principles require equal sharing of the surplus generated unless there is good reason to depart; greater financial contribution alone is not such a reason.
legal_issues: Application of White v White to short childless marriages where both parties worked
Whether unequal capital contributions justify unequal division of profits
Scope of appellate intervention in ancillary relief after Cordle v Cordle
Treatment of pre-marital property such as Rectory Lane

enrichment.short_title: VAT on long-term seasonal caravan park pitches upheld
key_facts: Colaingrove operated 22 UK caravan parks letting about 14,500 seasonal pitches to caravan owners for holiday use rather than permanent residence.
The VAT Tribunal held pitch lettings were taxable; Colaingrove appealed, arguing the UK rules exceeded EU law.
The dispute centred on whether seasonal pitches fell within the hotel-sector exclusion or a valid Member State derogation under the Article 13B tailpiece.
Jacob J held the matter acte claire and dismissed the appeal.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the High Court from the VAT Tribunal on validity of UK VAT treatment of seasonal caravan pitches.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; no reference to the Court of Justice.
enrichment.ratio: Member States have a wide discretion under the Article 13B(b) tailpiece of the Sixth VAT Directive to exclude lettings from the immovable property exemption; taxing seasonal caravan pitches that are not dwellings is within that discretion and is not irrational compared with long-stay hotel treatment.
legal_issues: Whether UK taxation of seasonal caravan pitches is permitted under Article 13B of the Sixth Directive
Scope of the Member State tailpiece power to exclude lettings from exemption
Whether Lubbock Fine requires equivalent transactions to be treated identically
Whether a reference to the ECJ was required

enrichment.short_title: NMW enforcement notices limited to current workers
key_facts: Bebb Travel employed coach stewards who sold refreshments and were treated as below the minimum wage when sales profits were excluded.
All stewards were dismissed in May 2000 and an Inland Revenue enforcement officer later served a section 19 notice requiring back pay for 25 former workers.
The Employment Tribunal and Employment Appeal Tribunal held the notice invalid because it related only to past workers and past pay periods.
The Inland Revenue appealed, arguing section 19(2) allowed standalone recovery for past underpayments.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal with permission from the Employment Appeal Tribunal on construction of section 19.
enrichment.ratio: Section 19(2) of the National Minimum Wages Act 1998 is supplemental to section 19(1) and permits back-pay requirements only in an enforcement notice served on a worker who currently qualifies; there is no power to issue an enforcement notice solely in respect of former workers.
legal_issues: Whether section 19(2) is freestanding or parasitic on section 19(1)
Meaning of a worker who qualifies for the national minimum wage in section 19(1)
Whether past workers may be the subject of enforcement notices and daily penalties
Purposive construction of penal enforcement provisions

enrichment.short_title: University exclusion of disruptive research student upheld
key_facts: Mr Bangert, a research student at South Bank University, was excluded after Dr Farwell investigated allegations of disruptive conduct made by Professor Bridge.
Allegations included obstructive behaviour, unsatisfactory attendance, refusal to accept supervision changes, and publishing controversial material on the university website after 11 September 2001.
The claimant challenged the exclusion by judicial review, relying on a large volume of material not before the investigator.
Hooper J held the investigation was fair and that the finding on allegation 3 alone justified termination of the studentship.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application for judicial review of South Bank University's decision to terminate the claimant's studentship and exclude him from the university.
enrichment.outcome: Claim dismissed; application for permission to appeal refused; claimant ordered to pay costs.
enrichment.ratio: A university's disciplinary investigation and exclusion decision will not be quashed where the decision-maker properly applied internal procedures and there was overwhelming evidence supporting at least one serious allegation, even if some subsidiary findings are open to doubt.
legal_issues: Whether Dr Farwell's investigation breached natural justice or university policy
Whether the university failed to investigate the claimant's counter-complaint against Professor Bridge
Whether website publication allegations alone justified exclusion
Whether fresh material not before the investigator could support judicial review

key_facts: Arrowcroft applied for planning permission for a mixed business park, housing and golf course at Waterside Park, Audenshaw, allocated in Tameside's UDP under policy DEN1.
After a public inquiry the Inspector recommended approval, but the Secretary of State refused permission in November 2002 citing conflicts with DEN1(h), policies L3 and L12, PPG3 and emerging RPG13.
Arrowcroft challenged the decision under section 288, arguing misdirection on section 54A, RPG13 policy EC6, inadequate reasons, bias and irrationality.
The deputy judge rejected all seven grounds and refused permission to appeal.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application under section 288 of the Town and Country Planning Act 1990 to quash the Secretary of State's called-in planning decision.
enrichment.outcome: Application refused; permission to appeal refused; claimant ordered to pay the Secretary of State's costs.
enrichment.ratio: Under section 54A a proposal may be refused despite general conformity with a site-specific allocation if material considerations, including conflicting UDP policies and national guidance on brownfield use and leisure provision, outweigh the plan; the decision-maker is not required to follow a rigid two-stage formula or treat every policy breach as fatal to accordance with the plan as a whole.

Construction of emerging RPG13 policy EC6 and the NWDA strategic sites list
Adequacy of reasons on regeneration, housing under PPG3, golf provision and density

enrichment.short_title: University stress-at-work claim: leave to appeal refused
key_facts: Professor Foumeny, head of Leeds University's Chemical Engineering Department, resigned after restructuring proposals and later suffered psychiatric illness attributed to workplace stress.
He sued the university alleging deliberate harassment by senior managers during a unitary school merger and subsequent disciplinary process.

Judge Grenfell applied Hatton v Sutherland principles and found psychiatric injury was foreseeable from May 1997 but no breach of duty because reasonable steps were limited once restructuring and discipline were underway.
The Court of Appeal refused permission to appeal, criticising an extraneous finding on race discrimination not raised at trial.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application for permission to appeal to the Court of Appeal from a High Court judgment dismissing a negligence claim for stress-related psychiatric injury.
enrichment.ratio: An employer is not in breach of duty for stress-related psychiatric injury unless plainly foreseeable indications required reasonable preventative steps that were practicable in context; appellate intervention is unavailable where findings on motivation, foreseeability and breach were open to the trial judge on the evidence.
legal_issues: Foreseeability of psychiatric injury under Hatton v Sutherland
Whether university managers deliberately harassed the claimant or acted within restructuring and disciplinary procedures
What reasonable steps the university should have taken once stress became foreseeable
